explanations.answer: They obey the voice of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Haggai 1:12 says Zerubbabel, Joshua and all the remnant of the people “obeyed the voice of the LORD their God.” That's the governor, the high priest and everybody else, all on the same page. I've had a timer go off and still stood there staring at it, so this impresses me. They heard it, and they did it.

explanations.answer: They return to their own houses
explanations.explanation: That's what they'd been doing, since the LORD said each of them was busy with his own house (Haggai 1:9). But Haggai 1:12 says they obeyed the voice of the LORD. Going back home would be like hearing the oven buzzer and heading for the couch. Not this crowd, friend.

explanations.answer: They wait until the time has come
explanations.explanation: This one sounds familiar because the people had said the time had not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD (Haggai 1:2). But after hearing the message, Haggai 1:12 says they obeyed the voice of the LORD. I spent years waiting in the back of a junk drawer, so I respect a good wait. This just isn't one.

Haggai 1:12 says they obeyed his words “because the LORD their God had sent him.” Haggai 1:13 even calls him “the messenger of the LORD.” So the people weren't just hearing a man with an opinion. They were hearing the one the LORD sent.

Good guess, since the message was a serious one. But Haggai 1:12 doesn't use that word. It says the LORD their God had sent him, and that's the reason the verse gives for why they obeyed. I'm sticking with the word the verse picked, friend.

The word rebuked isn't in this verse. Haggai 1:12 says the LORD their God had sent him, and that's why they obeyed his words. I'll admit I'd have picked the dramatic word too. Dramatic words are my weakness.

Haggai 1:13 says Haggai delivered the message of the LORD: “I am with you,” declares the LORD. That's four little words, and they come right after the people obeyed. I think a baker could chew on those four words all day. Short and plain, and nothing missing.
Not in this passage. The message in Haggai 1:13 is “I am with you,” declares the LORD. No deadline and no weather report. I'd have stuck a timer on it myself, but the verse is just those four words.

These verses say nothing about size. What Haggai delivers in 1:13 is “I am with you,” declares the LORD. There's no blueprint and no measurements. If I'd been writing that message, I'd have added a dozen cookie-box specs.

Haggai 1:14 says, “So the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah…” Haggai delivered the message, but the LORD is the One who did the stirring. Zerubbabel's spirit got moved, and the verse tells us exactly who moved it.

Haggai is the messenger of the LORD (Haggai 1:13), and he's the one delivering the message. But Haggai 1:14 says the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel. Haggai handed over the words, and the stirring came from the LORD. I get the pick, though, since Haggai is the one doing all the talking.

Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, does get his spirit stirred in Haggai 1:14. But he's on the receiving end, right alongside Zerubbabel. The verse says the LORD stirred both of their spirits. Easy mix-up, since Joshua's name is parked right next to Zerubbabel's.

Not quite. Haggai 1:14 says the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel, and then adds Joshua the high priest, “as well as the spirit of all the remnant of the people.” The governor wasn't the only one. I get why his name jumped out, since he's listed first, like the biggest cookie on the tray.

You got it, baker. Haggai 1:14 says the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel the governor, and the spirit of Joshua the high priest, “as well as the spirit of all the remnant of the people.” Nobody got left out of the stirring. The whole crowd was in it.

Haggai 1:14 says “they came and began the work on the house of the LORD of Hosts, their God.” The spirits got stirred, and then hands got busy. Talking was done, and the work had started. That's the word the verse uses, and I love it.

Hold on, friend, nobody finishes anything on the first day. Haggai 1:14 says they came and began the work on the house of the LORD of Hosts. This verse is a starting line, and the finish isn't in it. Even I can't finish a whole bakery in a day, and my mustache has a lot of reach.

Nobody's walking around with a clipboard in this verse. Haggai 1:14 says they came and began the work on the house of the LORD of Hosts. They started the work itself. Inspecting would've been a fine way to spend a morning, but the verse has them picking up the work.

Haggai 1:15 puts the start on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius. That's a very exact date. I think a date that exact means somebody wanted this start remembered. The verse hands us the day, the month and the king.

Cyrus is the king of Persia named in Ezra 1:1, but he's not the king in this verse. Haggai 1:15 says the second year of King Darius. Kings with big names start to blur together for me. This verse pins it to Darius.

Artaxerxes is another king of Persia (Ezra 7:1), but he isn't named in this passage. Haggai 1:15 puts the start in the second year of King Darius. I'd have bet on a king too, since the verse names one. It just names a different one.
